speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. My guest today is Shiva Rajaraman, Chief Product and Technology Officer at MrBeast. Look at the logos: eight years at Google and YouTube, then Spotify, CTO at WeWork, Commerce at Meta, OpenSea, Uber. Now he builds the product behind 520 million subscribers and 1.6 billion views in 90 days. Here's the shift: at every platform before this, he built the canvas for other people's creativity. Here, the product is the output itself. Here are the things we'll cover: why they threw out enterprise SaaS and built their own tooling in three months; forward deployed engineers pointed inward at their own teams; shipping daily because an idea is now a prompt, not a backlog ticket; founders ship products designed for themselves, and how AI fixes that; and the memory layer, so a new hire inherits ten years of what went wrong. Let's get into it. [Sponsor]  AI helps us generate ideas, draft plans, and spin up work in minutes. But faster doesn't necessarily mean better. When everyone has their own AI tools, their own outputs, and their own context, you get fragmentation: fractured version control, scattered review processes, decisions happening in parallel, not in concert. Rebuilding context between people and platforms costs you time and momentum. That's where Mural comes in. Mural gives teams a shared visual canvas to bring work together. You can generate structured starting points right on the canvas instead of moving outputs between tools, keep all of your context in one place, and compatible AI agents can contribute alongside the team, bringing in context from the tools they already know. The future of work is still human. Learn more at mural.co. How This Executive Role Is Different

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Shiva, I'm bringing you some water, because I'm going to make you talk.

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: Thank you.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Thank you for being a big contributor over these last years. I think we met when you were at Spotify. You had all the logos, right? Google, Spotify, WeWork, and Uber. I'm probably forgetting some at this point.

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: Yes. I fall in love with a lot of things, so we'll leave it at that.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: But now MrBeast. So I'm very curious to know, how is this executive role different from the other executive roles you've had in more traditional big tech?

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: Let me start with this: I've largely worked on platforms. So a lot of my perspective has always been, how do you serve a ton of creators? Frankly, you become a canvas for other people's creativity. You're not the source of that creativity yourself. So one of the unique things about this role is, how do we build products that in and of themselves are creative productions? That could be a variety of different things, but of course we create videos right now. So a lot of it is, what do you get to do when you're working with someone who's done fantastic, great work, has great ideas, and wants to do more of it? How do you productize that? That's really the challenge. What do you get to do differently when you're working with that creator? You can be a little bit more selfish toward those objectives. You can get very deep in the workflow and maybe change the workflow. When you work at a platform, you don't get to do that. It's really hard. So you have to think, in our world, our product is the output, not just the platform that enables the output. It's a very different way of thinking, and I don't want to pretend it's easy. I'm making a lot of adjustments too. Internal and External Products

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So as Chief Technology Officer, you oversee both internal and external products?

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: Yeah, we're splitting it into internal and external products, correct.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So what exactly are those products?

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: First, let's start with the fact that we have a ton of creative people at Beast Industries, and they're creating content every day. This is everything from writers to editors to set designers to people figuring out if something is even feasible. We often do things that are the first-ever type of thing happening in the world, so can you even do it? The physics of it becomes a question. We have all these specialized people who've learned to work together and produce a fantastic piece of content that drops every two weeks on MrBeast. But there are many more channels, and we also have our studio that's ramping up new channels that are separate from MrBeast. So one tool is: how do we create the workflow for all of those people, so we can move fast, produce at the highest quality, but stay on time and budget as well? In the past, I think all of you know this, you'd probably get some enterprise SaaS tool off the shelf. No offense to anyone in that world, but what we found is that every one of those project management tools just falls short in our world. So our question was, in the age of AI, can we actually just build the perfect tool for ourselves? That started about three months ago, and now you're seeing us ship every day. We see an issue with the studio, usually it's Jimmy and the studio teams saying, "what if we could do this?" And it turns out you can do just about anything in software right now, you don't have to worry about the cost of it, and you can maintain it very easily as well. So what we've ended up doing is looking at each of those tasks and building an operating system around it. What's exciting about that as an internal tool is that you never have to compromise anymore. So if, for example, we have people running around a set at midnight trying to make changes, they can just talk to their phone and record that stuff, rather than bust out a laptop or look for a mobile app. In the past, you couldn't just create that app easily. You'd have to negotiate with the vendor: is this on your roadmap? They'd come back and say, "you're the only customer that has people running around at midnight who can only use voice," so they're not going to do it. And you're stuck. But in today's world, I think this is a big opportunity for product managers. If you assume anything is possible and everything is almost zero cost, not entirely zero cost, which we can talk about, why not do it? That's the philosophy we're taking with internal tools. For external tools, I can't say too much, but we're launching a consumer app, which is very public out there. What we're excited about is: what can we do in that app that lets people in the real world, our fans who've consumed YouTube content for a long time, or content on Instagram and TikTok where we're also producing, do something more participatory? So we're spending time defining that and designing it. And as you can imagine, this is the peak AI period, so the ability to prototype, bring ideas to vision, and test those ideas quickly is what we're working on now. Turning Attention Into a Business

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Speaking of numbers, last time I checked, MrBeast has over 520 million subscribers just on YouTube, and over 1.5 billion viewers just in the last 90 days.

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: 1.6, yeah.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Exactly. So it's not a small thing.

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: It's pretty crazy.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: We talk about how attention is the new currency, and I'm curious to know your vision to convert that attention into a business, beyond the traditional ways you monetize.

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: Some of it is just the traditional way you monetize. If you have a large audience and you're sitting on an ad-supported platform, you can monetize that through deep sponsorships and advertising. That's obvious for most people. The question is, as we start to launch our own direct-to-consumer app, there are obviously different things we can play with there as well. We sell merchandise today. We could explore things like subscriptions. But all of that is secondary. Right now, the real question is, how can I engage you and really craft that engaging experience? If that takes off, we've got a nice, supportive foundation for exploring bets there. We'll find the right organic, blended way to monetize it, but we don't necessarily have to obsess about it now. The other advantage, and the theme here is how fast can you ship and produce, is that we want to test those monetization vectors. What can work here? What can work in a different market? We're global; our audience is all over the place. So what might work in the United States might be very different from what works in India. In the past, you might spread that over years of development. I think we have a chance to try different things in different pockets, see what sticks, and graduate the winners, not just on core product experiences, but on the monetization angle too. Working With Jimmy Without Making Him the Bottleneck

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: One thing that comes to mind as we think about bottlenecks is that a huge part of MrBeast's brand is actually Jimmy. So when you're working directly with him and he's involved in a lot of the details, and in fact he's on camera, how is it to work with him, and how do you find ways to make sure he doesn't become that bottleneck?

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: Good question. First, when you think about someone like Jimmy, he's an entrepreneur. He's created something over several years now that is just impressive, and that doesn't come from just creative thinking. To build an org that can sustain that, to build the muscle and the tactics to sustain that, you see a lot of product thinking there too. If you've seen him talk, it's totally worth it: how can you break down the creative successes into analytical recipes? How do we get that insight? How are we looking at that insight every day? Just like you might launch a product and do a product review ahead of it, then a retro after it ships, every video goes through that same process. So one thing is, it's actually not hard to work with someone like that, because they're thinking the way we think; it's in their DNA. The other side of it is just showing good judgment on workflow. There are people in the world who are creative but aren't very good at looking at the operations behind that creativity, trying to abstract it and see what's repeatable and what tools can make it happen. In our case, the company is obsessed with that as well. If you look at historical industries and how some creative workflows have evolved over time, many of them haven't changed in 50 years. If you're native to YouTube and you realize the pace and the bar you need to have, you start looking at each one of those: how do you onboard people, how do you train them, how do you get people experimenting with new tools, how do you give those people superpowers, how do you get rid of the mundane so they can focus on the magical aspects of what they do? That obsession is very good, and the instincts are there in the company to really understand that deeply. Part of that is just everyone running together all the time. When you see something going wrong, you ask yourself, is that a feature? If so, let's build it now. The weird thing about us is that it will turn into a meeting that night. There'll be some vibe coding overnight, prototype what it is, and it will ship the next day. Now, that can be exhausting, unless you rotate people into it, or have some people working in different time zones who can do this. But that pace, combined with the observation of what's working or not, bringing that together, is very exciting. I hope many more companies work like that. Forward Deployed Engineers, Pointed Inward

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: One way to look at that, and you give a talk on this too, is that internally within our company, we effectively have forward deployed engineers in the functions. There's a couple who can sit there and prototype and solve problems for the studio, and we can do that in marketing and other areas as well. A lot of people have talked about forward deployed engineers with your client base. It's interesting for us to think about them internally deployed, and how they can pick up the speed and insights very quickly, because they live and breathe with the people they support. The difference is they can prototype something very quickly as a solution. And because it's so cheap to prototype, you can try ten different things, find which one works, and throw away the one that doesn't. That motion is very new to me, actually, but I'm finding it to be very liberating, and something we should all think about in our own companies.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I want to double down on that, because even to me, shipping on a weekly basis is already fast. You mentioned you're shipping on a daily basis. So how does that actually work?

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: Internally, shipping on a daily basis just means you're being very responsive to people's needs. You see an issue, and I'll keep picking on enterprise SaaS, I don't mean to, SaaS is evolving as well, but one of the things I remember throughout my career working with vendors is you'd have that quarterly QBR or review, if you're a major client: here are the things we want on the roadmap. Too much of the time was spent justifying it, making the case for it. In today's world, the importance of shipping every day is that, hey, there's something broken, or what if we had this filter, or this view? What if that view looked completely different from a Gantt chart, but was much more usable for our teams and simpler, so they can just glance at it on a big screen, because that's the nature of our work? We can just ship that. So what ends up happening is: ship it, get feedback, and if it doesn't work, kill it, iterate on it, take a different direction. That's all very cheap right now. So shipping every day, the way to look at it is, it's the equivalent of, in the past, taking all these features and putting them on a board. Instead, if you take all those features, you're not putting them on a board and prioritizing them later; you're just taking those ideas and turning them into prompts. Then you throw those prompts out there and see what spits back. "Hey, that's kind of interesting, let's iterate on it." "Okay, let's throw it out there." So you're just compressing time. It makes the product challenge even more important. You have to know what problem you're solving, and if you have 50 things all going out there, you could confuse your user base very quickly. So sometimes it's about packaging it up a little bit more, but sometimes it's also, hey, this is for this department, this skill, a very specific view, there are ten of them, just get it out there and see what happens. So we balance that as we think about shipping every day. What Makes Legendary Founder Cultures Special

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: As you were saying that, I was thinking about culture. You've had first-hand experience working with some legendary founders and experiencing the cultures they created. Founder of WeWork, founder of Spotify, founder of Meta, now founder of MrBeast. I put Jimmy at that level. So what is it that you see there that makes those types of cultures so special?

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: One thing you're seeing, and there's been a lot of talk about this, but I think it's true, is that what drives a lot of these founders is the same thing that drives a good product manager: I wish I could ship faster. I wish I could try five ideas out, optionality, instead of one. I wish I knew how to do X and didn't have to buy it, but could build it and control it myself. So what you see with a lot of those founders is that they believe that's just the way it should be. And I would argue that in the last six months, they've all finally gotten the world they wished for. If you think about your worst times as a product manager, you have to pick one choice. You have a huge set of options in front of you, but because of engineering scarcity, because of how long it takes, because of what it takes to make that robust and secure, you only get to pick one thing, and it would have been better to do three. So great founders force that in their own organization: can we do it fast? It can be very annoying, by the way. "Can we do it faster? Why can't we just do it? I can vibe code anything now." But if you really put yourself in the product position, we've been trying to play that role for 25 years now, in my case, and you're like, oh my gosh, this is crazy. So right now, what we have to do is shift our behavior. When I was in certain roles, I was like, "oh, we've got to prioritize A, B, and C." The founder relationship can be very tense, because you're trying to justify one path versus five, because you have real scarcity. But in a world where you don't have that scarcity anymore, you're probably asking yourself a different question. "We've got three ideas here. Have we actually explored the full option space, or are three ideas enough?" That's really the question now. Should we really be exploring ten? How fast can we do that? And what are our principles to guide that? So it's a very different role you're playing. A year from now, you might be able to explore even more options.

speaker: The Founder Blind Spot AI Fixes Shiva Rajaraman
text: Now you've got a different issue, which is judgment. One of the questions is, you have to look at your founder and say, where are their strengths, but where are their blind spots? And if you're a product leader working with those types of people, you need to ask yourself, how do I fill the blind spots while they focus on their strengths? With every founder I've worked with or been close to, even indirectly, they all have major strengths. They also have major blind spots, and one of the biggest blind spots for most founders is they often design a product for themselves, not for the broader set of users. So what you can do now with AI is: let's do that, the founder's version, but let's also create two varieties based on what I understand about the user needs. Now we've got all three, and you don't have to make that choice. In the past, you'd have to make that choice, and guess who wins in that choice? The founder's choice. And not too often, but so many products, at every place I've worked, have shipped and launched a product designed for the founder, not for the users, and failed for that reason. So I think that's what's changing too. Sorry, I'm rambling, but you get the idea. The force of AI gives you this superpower of exploration that is firmly in the hands of the product team and others involved, product in quotes. How do you use that now to get a better result? That's really what we need to figure out over the next year. Speed wins, but so does breadth of option space, and really thinking through that also has to go with speed. Otherwise you might just go down the wrong path very fast. So that's the part we need to figure out. Applying AI to the Creative Process

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I want to explore that with some examples, because I remember even before AI was mainstream, Jimmy was talking about how he was so obsessed with experimenting with YouTube thumbnails, titles, images, different facial expressions. So fast-forward four years, with the tools now at your disposal, how are you actually applying AI in specific parts of the process to turbocharge that acceleration?

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: The main reason we use AI is largely to make sure that process is all connected. You could think of it largely as workflow: you have an ideation team, which is very good at all the things you talked about, what's the title, what's the thumbnail. Then, okay, now I need to come up with a bunch of storylines for this, and then I've got to design the sets for that. So there's a sequence of things that happen, and it's been very disconnected. So putting that in one system means you can see where the source of a delay is. How do I learn that a particular set I designed, what if a whole new team is working on a set later? There's no memory layer in these organizations unless you all meet. And if you're moving very fast, that's a problem. So why not put that memory layer in the AI side of things? "Hey, I know you're trying to do this set, and it involves a huge tub, and we're going to fill it with something to make it look like whatever. Here are the three things you need to remember. By the way, if you do this one thing, it's not going to work." That should just be instantaneous now. So one way to look at it is: there are a hundred people running around all day, running into problems, running into solutions, and we're just making that available, so the next time you pop in an idea, it comes back and tells you what to watch out for. That's a very concrete way of doing it, and I think that's the most interesting thing. Of course, people are using tools everywhere in the world right now to do creative workflows. What's more interesting for us is, how do we take the knowledge that often might be sitting in one person's head and make that knowledge available to everyone? So every video, every production, all the errors that can make it go wrong are no longer surprises. If you join the team on day one, you should have the history of everyone who's worked on this for ten years, and that should be available to you. Then we should refine that history as we learn things too. So what's been very interesting with AI is how you should institutionalize that forced capture of everything, so all those nuggets of knowledge are put into one place, and then you're voting up or down on whether that knowledge makes sense across everything or is localized to something. Once that base is built, you'll see exponential returns on that wisdom. That's the most important aspect of what we're doing, in my opinion.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Shiva, we're going to leave it with that. Thank you so much for being part of it.

speaker: Shiva Rajaraman
text: Thank you.
